content.intro: Explore custom request and response behavior through the source syllabus topics, a small inspectable example, and a practical verification task. The example is teaching material, not a claim that the platform executed Flask code.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Custom Request and Response Behavior matters because it helps a Flask application keep its request/response behavior explicit and testable as the surrounding project grows. Learners should understand the responsibility, when to use it, and its failure boundaries instead of only memorizing an API call.

content_blocks.title: What to learn
content_blocks.text: This lesson covers: Extending request or response classes; Custom serialization or parsing behavior; Compatibility and maintenance considerations. Keep the source terms intact; for each one, name the component that owns the behavior, the inputs/assumptions, and the expected result.

items.title: Extending request or response classes
items.text: Trace which parts of the incoming request are trusted, which are optional, and how invalid data maps to a response.

items.title: Custom serialization or parsing behavior
items.text: Use custom serialization or parsing behavior as a named design decision: note the assumptions, the normal path, and one boundary case to test.

items.title: Compatibility and maintenance considerations
items.text: When applying compatibility and maintenance considerations, keep the implementation small, document version-dependent behavior, and verify it with a focused check.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Custom Request and Response Behavior
content_blocks.code:
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.get("/api/status")
def status():
    response = jsonify({"status": "ok"})
    response.headers["Cache-Control"] = "no-store"
    return response, 200
content_blocks.expected_output: GET /api/status returns HTTP 200 with a JSON body and Cache-Control: no-store.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run the app locally and inspect the response status, content type, body, and headers in a browser or API client.

content_blocks.title: Before using this beyond practice
content_blocks.text: Validate untrusted input at the server boundary, keep secrets out of source code, and test the failure path. Optional extensions or hosting infrastructure are separate dependencies unless stated otherwise.

troubleshooting: Confirm the expected virtual environment and installed dependency versions before diagnosing framework behavior.

For database or third-party integration examples, use isolated local resources and explicit timeouts; do not use production credentials.

content.try_it_yourself: Apply custom request and response behavior to a tiny local Flask app. Predict what a normal request should do, test one invalid or boundary case, and record expected versus observed behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a fragment without checking its imports, app configuration or dependencies.
common_mistakes.why: Many Flask examples assume a configured app and a specific runtime or extension version.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the run instructions, record the Flask/Python version and test the smallest behavior first.

common_mistakes.problem: Checking only the successful request path.
common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, unsupported methods, unauthorized objects and service failures often have different behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a negative or boundary test and assert the status code and response contract.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a local example as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Secret management, concurrency, deployment, monitoring and failure recovery need separate design decisions.
common_mistakes.fix: Review the matching deployment and security references before publication or real use.
